We need to prepare a clarified explanation of sanitization here: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x10-V1-Encoding-and-Sanitization.md#v13-sanitization

This is in response to issues including:
* https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3236
* https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3208
* https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3237
* https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3245

comments.body:
Ok, so here's the deal. 

In ASVS we talk about input validation as a control that gets applied very early on as a business logic step that ensures that a data item being received is correct (from a business perspective) for that type of data.

We separately talk about sanitization as a control of last resort where encoding and escaping is not possible. Up until now, we have mostly referred to this as a "blocklist" control where dangerous characters are stripped out. This has received criticism in a bunch of recent issues from people including @ajayojha, @jmanico and @narfbg for being bypassable.

I think the solution here is to include a clarification in this section that the best sanitization should be allowlist based with a blocklist only being used if there is no other alternative.

This is different to escaping and encoding because it is changing the actual representation of the data (remember sanitization is the last resort from a security perspective) and it is different to input validation because that is a business logic control where this sanitization is happening to make content safe in a particular context. This differentiation is why I prefer not to confuse things by  talking about validation here.

So, if we make it very clear that sanitization should be allowlist based with a blocklist only being used if there is no other alternative, do you think that fixes our concerns about this term?

@jmanico @elarlang @ajayojha @narfbg

We just need to make this phrase correct
> removing potentially dangerous characters or content

and change it to the meaning
> keep only know-to-be-safe characters or content

For the wider context, allow-list vs block-list is not only a sanitization problem, but it can also be a problem in input validation. The difference is only how the application behaves when incorrect input comes - modifies it to be "safe" (sanitization) or rejects the request (validation)

> So, if we make it very clear that sanitization should be allowlist based with a blocklist only being used if there is no other alternative, do you think that fixes our concerns about this term?

I recommend adding a warning statement along these lines, some of which ASVS is covering already:

Incorrect or overly broad sanitization can weaken security and must not be used as a substitute for proper validation, encoding, or escaping.

- Sanitization is acceptable only as a last-resort, context-specific control
- It should be allowlist-based
- It should never be implied as a general injection defense
- Poor sanitization can actively create security flaws

Even well-implemented sanitization libraries like DOMPurify have a legitimate but narrow role. It renders user-supplied HTML where you genuinely need to preserve markup. Outside that specific use case, encoding is almost always the better choice.

My comment on memcache also expresses some concern considering validation to only be a business logic issue.

https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3208#issuecomment-3986305583

There are cases where validation is not a business logic issue, but a security control where no other alternative is the right call.

For example, path traversal is primarily a validation problem because the attacker is not “injecting code into an interpreter” (where output encoding would fix semantics), and they’re not merely supplying “bad characters” that can be safely stripped. They are supplying an alternative resource identifier. A path that changes what object the program selects. That’s a control decision, and control decisions are solved by constraining the allowed set, i.e., validation.

The allow/deny clarification might help, a little, but I don't think it's realistically solving a problem.

For one, there's a chicken and egg problem in that if you already have a complete known-to-be-safe list of characters or patterns, then I see no legitimate reason why validation or context-aware escaping wouldn't be possible.

Secondly, this is nobody's fault and I am admittedly being cynical about it - developers just go "that's the same thing" and write blacklists anyway. I've seen it time and time again. Even after a major incident once, I still had engineering managers asking me "What's easier?" as if it's a gotcha argument in favor of blacklists.

And finally, even the perfect implementation is inherently damaging data integrity. This almost always has unpredictable second-order effects, which then cascade cascade further and are extremely hard to spot or debug. By the time you figure out the root cause, the whole system already depends on the broken behavior, so there's no will to fix it. Security gets the blame regardless.

These things aren't obvious, but should show that finding a "right way" to do sanitization is futile. Putting more emphasis on warning against its dangers would be more productive IMO.

@narfbg - ASVS must be understandable and easy to read as possible, but it can not and does not aim to fill the knowledge gap, lack of security knowledge for developers or historical stupid decisions.

@elarlang I agree with that.

However, it should discourage poor practices (i.e. sanitization), and currently it isn't doing a great job at that. While this isn't intentional, having an entire section with 12 requirements that instruct to sanitize is leading in the opposite direction. That's the main problem for me.

> [@elarlang](https://github.com/elarlang) I agree with that.
> 
> However, it should discourage poor practices (i.e. sanitization), and currently it isn't doing a great job at that. While this isn't intentional, having an entire section with 12 requirements that instruct to sanitize is leading in the opposite direction. That's the main problem for me.

I agree 100%. I'm also concerned that we are not using the terms validation, encoding and sanitization for the right purposes. We have reduced validation to business logic only, and we conflated the definition of sanitization. I think it's  good idea to fix both of these.

Thanks all for the detailed feedback. Let me try and address the different points raised.

**On the use of the term "validation" in this context**

I want to be careful about introducing "validation" terminology into this section, because across the security industry, "validation" is overwhelmingly associated with input validation, i.e., checking that incoming data conforms to expected formats and business rules. Introducing it into a section about making content safe for a specific output context risks confusing readers.

**On the path traversal example**

@jmanico, the path traversal example is an interesting one, but I'd note that OWASP's own path traversal guidance recommends **path canonicalization** (resolving the path and verifying it starts with the expected base directory) as the primary defense. That is closer to normalization/encoding than input validation. The allowlisting of permitted filenames is a supplementary layer, and when applied at the input stage, it is input validation (covered by V2.2). When applied at the point of use, it is context-specific sanitization (covered by V1.3). The current taxonomy handles this correctly.

**On the core proposal: allowlist-based sanitization**

Based on the feedback, here is what I'm proposing for the V1.3 section clarification:

1. **Sanitization should be allowlist-first.** The current phrasing about "removing potentially dangerous characters" implies blocklist thinking. As @elarlang suggested, we should reframe this to "keeping only known-to-be-safe characters or content." Even DOMPurify, a good example of well-implemented sanitization, works on an allowlist basis: you configure which tags and attributes are permitted.

2. **Blocklist-based sanitization is an even further last resort.** If you cannot define a safe allowlist, a blocklist approach may still be better than nothing, but this is the weakest form of defense and should be clearly labeled as such.

3. **Sanitization remains a last resort overall.** The hierarchy should be clear: use encoding/escaping first. Only use sanitization when you genuinely need to preserve some form of the content but encoding alone cannot make it safe (rich HTML being the classic example). And when you do sanitize, prefer allowlist over blocklist.

**On the concern about 12 requirements "normalizing" sanitization**

@narfbg, @jmanico, I hear the concern that having a whole section with 12 requirements could send the wrong signal. I think that's worth looking at separately. Some of those requirements might benefit from rewording to emphasize the specific encoding or parameterization approach rather than the generic word "sanitize." But I'd like to treat that as a follow-up, separate to getting the section introduction right. Practically speaking, these items are here because we have judged that encoding, escaping or parameterization are not possible in these cases.

For now, I'd like to focus on getting agreement on the explanatory text: sanitization is a last resort, it should be allowlist-first, and blocklist sanitization should only be used when there truly is no other option.

Does this direction work for everyone?

#3208 raises a different question.

Are there situations where we want to do rejection rather than “sanitize and continue.”

I think rejection is very possible at the input validation stage because at that point we are only just receiving the content.

However, when it comes to using previously received content in a specific, security-sensitive context, I think that rejecting risks breaking the application because the application functionality is relying on using the content in that way. For this reason, I am not sure rejection is a good idea at this stage.

The standard path traversal defense is two-step: step one is normalization/canonicalization, but step two is validation/authorization of the resolved resource.

This is not encoding in the traditional sense. We are not transforming the input for safe output rendering. We normalize the path to a single canonical form so we can validate it correctly (for example, that it stays within an expected base directory), and then we use the canonicalized result.

* Encoding transforms data for safe use in a specific output context.
* Sanitization modifies data to remove or neutralize disallowed content.
* Validation accepts or rejects data based on whether it meets rules/constraints.

Preventing path traversal is therefore primarily a validation control (a boundary check on the canonical path), not encoding and not sanitization.

Sanitization as we’ve described is often dangerous, but there are use cases where it’s necessary. 

Validation is not always sufficient by itself, but it is necessary in certain cases. Validation is also used for business rules, but it’s sometimes essential for security as well.

Also Josh, normalization and output encoding are very different things.

* Normalization is not a type of encoding. Output encoding transforms data into a safer representation for a rendering context. Normalization is converting data into a canonical form to enable accurate validation; it may include decoding and resolution steps (e.g., ./.., separators, symlinks), but it is not encoding and it is not sanitization (i.e., it’s not “removing bad characters”).

If you permanently modify input to make it "safe to consume," that falls under sanitization: the act of modifying data for security.

> However, when it comes to using previously received content in a specific, security-sensitive context, I think that rejecting risks breaking the application because the application functionality is relying on using the content in that way. For this reason, I am not sure rejection is a good idea at this stage.

From a Zero Trust architecture perspective, inputs must be validated at every stage of processing. Any layer that consumes data becomes a new trust boundary and must independently verify that the data is safe for its specific use.

If validation fails at a deeper layer, rejection is often the correct and necessary response. Systems must be designed to safely handle invalid or malicious input at any stage of execution.

If rejecting unsafe input at a later stage breaks the application, that typically indicates a design flaw. In those cases, the correct fix is to improve the system’s data handling and validation model rather than attempting to repair, sanitize, or mutate the data to make it acceptable.

**_In security-sensitive contexts, rejecting invalid input is frequently safer and more reliable than attempting to transform untrusted data into a supposedly safe form._**

This concept is described in several documents like NIST SP 800-207, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, NIST SP 800-160, NIST SP 800-218, NIST SP 800-95 and NIST SP 800-204A.

> This concept is described in several documents like NIST SP 800-207, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, NIST SP 800-160, NIST SP 800-218, NIST SP 800-95 and NIST SP 800-204A.

If Jim points to standards, I have historical reasons to ask precise quotes :)

In general, I see that here is an AI-boosted philosophy with questionable progress. I also point out that we have a catch-all-sanitization requirement, which is quite clear with the intent:
> v5.0.0-1.3.3 Verify that data being passed to a potentially dangerous context is sanitized beforehand to enforce safety measures, **such as only allowing characters which are safe for this context** and trimming input which is too long.

> If Jim points to standards, I have historical reasons to ask precise quotes :)

The concept of re-validating at every tier is a very basic one. You do not need quotes.

> In general, I see that here is an AI-boosted philosophy 

Absolutely it is and I suggest you read it. The concept of re-validating at every tier is again a very basic one and I'm surprised we are having this debate. So since it was challenged, I brought out the big guns to explain it to you in more detail.

Thanks for the continued discussion. Let me respond to the points raised.

### On path traversal and normalization vs. encoding

@jmanico, fair point. Normalization and encoding are different operations and I should not have conflated them.

### On rejection vs. sanitization

I think we are actually more aligned here than it might appear. On the question of rejection at the point of use: I am open to considering this, but I would like to see concrete examples. V1.3 covers situations where data that has already been accepted into the system is being used in a potentially dangerous context. In those situations, can you point to specific cases where rejecting at the point of use (rather than sanitizing) is practical? Bearing in mind that the data has already been stored and the application is relying on using it. I can see the argument in principle, but I want to understand the practical scenarios before we add it to the guidance.

### On the NIST references

@jmanico, please avoid quoting standards unless you have clear guidance from them to support your point. From a quick review of the standards you quoted:

- **SP 800-207** (Zero Trust) is about authentication and authorization for resource access ("never trust, always verify"). It does not discuss data content validation at every processing tier.
- **SP 800-53 SI-10** (Information Input Validation) covers validating inputs at system boundaries and prescreening before passing to interpreters, but does not describe re-validation at every internal layer.
- **SP 800-218** (SSDF), **SP 800-160** (Systems Security Engineering), **SP 800-95** (Secure Web Services), and **SP 800-204A** (Microservices) do not appear to specifically address multi-tier data content validation either.

If you have specific sections or quotes from these documents that address data validation/rejection at every processing tier (as distinct from access control verification), I would genuinely like to see them, as it would be useful for the ASVS.

Also, saying "this is a basic point" without digging into the specific subtlties of the point we are discussing is a little patronising.

(Full disclosure, I am currently using Claude Code to help analyse and respond to issues but I am also carefully reviewing responses.)

### Overall

I hear the concerns about whether validation should have a security role beyond business logic, and whether the terminology taxonomy needs a rethink. These are worth exploring, but the direction depends on what we conclude about rejection having already accepted the content to begin with. If there is clear evidence that rejection is practical and appropriate for data already accepted into the system, then we would need to think about how to introduce a "security validation" concept into V1.3. If not, then I think we can proceed with the current framing: sanitization (allowlist-preferred) as the control for making content safe in a dangerous context.

So let us settle the rejection question first, and then decide on the taxonomy.

The purpose of validation is to ensure intentional format correctness, regardless of abstraction layers or domain boundaries. Format often happens to be determined by business logic, and this overlap is useful to push security into business logic layers, but that's circumstantial ... it doesn't define input validation as something that only belongs in business logic.

I think there's some legacy think remaining from the days of monoliths and perimeter defense as the main paradigm. Software was also not running the entire world, so it was easier to think that whatever potential problems might appear from mangling data (sanitization), they'd be rare, not have severe consequences, and be relatively easy to fix.

But modern applications have many integration points, are built from many components, the term application itself is often used to describe what's actually a system of interconnected applications. The complexity alone demands that faulty behavior (i.e. improperly formatted data) is rejected, because otherwise it spirals out of control.

For this reason, I am not sure rejection is a good idea at this stage."_

And my point is, if you cannot validate (and potentially reject data) at every tier of an application, then that is in itself a weakness. The idea that input validation should occur at every tier — at every trust boundary — is not controversial. It is one of the most thoroughly codified principles in security engineering.

I'll reply to sanitization in a different comment.

**_Sanitization attempts to remove or neutralize dangerous content from otherwise acceptable input. This almost always relies on a blacklist-style model, where the system tries to identify and strip known-bad patterns._**

This is a fairly standard definition (and use in code) of sanitization tools like DOMPurify. 

I worry that if we try to redefine sanitization beyond this core definition then we'll be going against the current conventional use of that term. And part of getting sanitization right as a term is getting validation right as a term. That's why these conversations are mixing together.

Good choice to use human-written comments :)

About "we go controversial with the industry" - as I wrote before (https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3335#issuecomment-3985251820) - in the old-and-not-that-good-days it was more common to use block-list also for input validation. Now it is (more) common sense that input validation is allow-list based. And the difference between "sanitization" vs "validation" is still only modification vs rejection.

So, I'm not worried about going against "the industry" definition. There are so many "terms" and definitions that "the industry" uses incorrectly, but I'll not start that list here.

Elar, these terms are already difficult enough, and changing their definitions only makes things more confusing for everyone.

What makes these terms especially challenging is that they are sometimes important security controls, but often they are not.

For that reason, I prefer not to rely on the terms alone. Instead, I try to explain precisely what is meant in the specific context. Clarifying what we mean by sanitization and what we mean by validation on a case-by-case basis is usually far more productive.

In practice, these terms are rarely helpful for defenders unless the exact mechanism and intent are clearly defined.

**So not only are we changing the definitions of sanitization and validation, we are also refusing to explain what we mean in context. That is a bad combination, and it makes an already confusing discussion even harder to follow.**
We can just use "allow-list based sanitization" and "allow-list based input validation". Should be clear enough.

Prepending “allow-list based” to both terms does not resolve the problem. It makes it worse, because it obscures a critical distinction.

Allow-list based input validation means checking whether input conforms to an expected formula and rejecting it outright if it does not. The input is never modified. Invalid input fails. This is a security gate.

Allow-list based sanitization means transforming input to remove or neutralize dangerous content while attempting to preserve the rest. The input is modified and passed through. This is a security filter.

These are fundamentally different operations. Calling them both “allow-list based” and expecting that to be “clear enough” is precisely the kind of ambiguity a verification standard should eliminate, not introduce.

Many engineers instead use a stricter model:
- validation = accept/reject unchanged input
- sanitization = destructive transformation

> Input validation happens at trust boundaries and is based on business rules for what makes sense for that data, not prevention of a specific vulnerability.

I disagree with the claim that input validation is only about business rules and not about preventing specific vulnerabilities.

Input validation absolutely serves business and domain correctness, but in some cases it is also a direct security control against concrete vulnerability classes. It is not always sufficient on its own, but it is still security-relevant.

A very clear example comes from OAuth 2.0 security guidance. RFC 9700 describes “Insufficient Redirection URI Validation” as a security weakness that let's an attacker obtain an authorization code or access token. In other words, improper validation of redirect URIs is directly tied to critical exploitable security outcomes, including open redirect abuse and token theft.

RFC 9700 does not treat this as a business-rule validation. It explicitly recommends exact redirection URI matching in section 4.1.3 https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html#name-countermeasures and says the authorization server must ensure the two URIs are equal, pointing to RFC 3986 Section 6.2.1 on simple string comparison, a form of input validation. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html#name-countermeasures 

So in my opinion, a more accurate statement is: Input validation is often driven by business and semantic rules, but in security-sensitive contexts it can also be a primary control for preventing specific vulnerabilities.

PS: Also take a look at the NIST control family for input validation from 800-53 (last updated August 2025). 
https://csf.tools/reference/nist-sp-800-53/r5/si/si-10/ It explicitly describes inter-component communication as requiring validation, not just user-facing input.

### On the OAuth redirect URI example

@jmanico, I agree that this is a good example where validation can serve as a direct security control. However, the OAuth redirect URI case is validation at the point of entry: the authorization server checks the URI when it arrives in the request. This is similar to the [WYSIWYG example I gave above](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/3335#issuecomment-4019252498).

In [10.4.1](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x19-V10-OAuth-and-OIDC.md#v104-oauth-authorization-server), we say:

"_Verify that the authorization server validates redirect URIs based on a client-specific allowlist of pre-registered URIs using exact string comparison._"

However this is not a case where data that has already been accepted and stored, is later used in a context where some of its content could be dangerous. In the OAuth case, the URI is validated before any action is taken, so there is nothing to reject later. @ajayojha seems to be backing up my point saying:

"_Rejecting stored data at a later stage can break application behavior if that content is already relied upon by the application._"

You said:

"_Input validation is often driven by business and semantic rules, but in security-sensitive contexts it can also be a primary control for preventing specific vulnerabilities._"

I would modify that to say:

"_Input validation is often driven by business and semantic rules, but in security-sensitive contexts it can also be a primary control for preventing specific vulnerabilities **if the input being received is being used exclusively in a particular security-sensitive context, such as in the redirect URL for an OAuth flow or for stored HTML content.**_"

### On the NIST SP 800-53 SI-10 reference

I had a look at SI-10 and its enhancements. It primarily addresses input validation at system boundaries, covering semantic and syntactic checking of inputs. The part where it talks about communication between components is in the context of "well-defined protocols that use structured messages", which is closer to input validation than to rejection of stored data at point of use.

It is also worth noting that SI-10's own description conflates input validation with injection prevention (it states "Input validation ensures accurate and correct inputs and prevents attacks such as cross-site scripting and a variety of injection attacks"), which is exactly the kind of terminological imprecision that ASVS is trying to avoid. XSS is primarily prevented through output encoding, not input validation.

So SI-10 seems to be focused on validation at boundaries rather than on the question of what to do with data already accepted into the system.

### Suggestion to resolve the issue

I agree with @ajayojha's suggestion to evaluate which V1.3 requirements genuinely need sanitization as the primary control. I think we can expand the 1.3 section text to refer to the specific conditions under which validation may be possible and then we can look at the items in 1.3 one by one to decide whether it is likely that "validate and reject" would be relevant in that situation or whether we would need to fall back on "sanitize and pass onwards" (allowlist or blocklist based).

1) Here are other examples where input validation is a primary security control in the world of standards (see below). I know this is a long list. If you would like exact citations in these standards I can get them. Not all of these references are perfect, but some are solid.

2) SI-10's is a reference to NIST's primary control standard as an over-arching standard at NIST where it cites input validation is a security control. _**When you validate data to numerics in typesafe languages, or validate strictly to [A-Za-z0-9] you get injection protection.**_ It's not elegant, but especially in number heavy systems, validation can be a critical control. 

**NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF v1.1)** is pretty direct here. It explicitly says, “Validate all inputs, and validate and properly encode all outputs” as part of secure coding practice under PW.5.1. That appears in a section focused on reducing software security vulnerabilities.

**WebAuthn Level 3 is another good example.** It relies on security-critical validation during authentication. The relying party is expected to verify that origin is an expected origin and that the rpIdHash matches the RP ID it expects. The spec also requires that the RP ID match the origin’s effective domain, or a registrable domain suffix of it. That is validation being used directly for security.

**FAPI 2.0 Security Profile (Final, 2025)** is another recent example from the OAuth space. It is a high-security profile for protecting sensitive APIs, especially in finance, and it explicitly follows the recommendations in RFC 9700.

**More broadly, in banking and financial systems**, input validation is often used as a fraud and transaction-integrity control. Validation checks are done on account identifiers, message structure, transaction fields, routing details, and protocol verification. These are not merely business-rule validation. When input validation is used to enforce security constraints and block fraudulent or malicious transactions, it is being used as a security control.

**RFC 8725** JWT Best Current Practices (2020, BCP 225) is the foundational document. Section 3.1 requires that libraries MUST enable callers to specify a supported set of algorithms and MUST NOT use any other algorithm. This is allow-list validation as security control.

**RFC 9068** JWT Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens (2021) builds on 8725 with six MUST-level checks in §4: the typ header MUST equal at+jwt, Medium the iss claim MUST exactly match the authorization server's issuer identifier, the aud claim MUST contain the resource server's identifier, alg value of none MUST be rejected, signature MUST be validated per RFC 7515, and current time MUST precede exp. 

**RFC 9449** DPoP (2023) contains the most enumerated validation checklist in the OAuth ecosystem. Section 4.3 specifies ten distinct MUST-level checks: single DPoP header presence, well-formed JWT structure, all required claims present, typ equals dpop+jwt, alg indicates a registered asymmetric algorithm and is not none, signature verifies against the embedded public key, the jwk parameter contains no private key material, htm matches the HTTP method, and htu matches the request URI. RFC Editor Refresh token binding to the DPoP key MUST be validated on subsequent presentations.

**RFC 9396** Rich Authorization Requests (2023) mandates comprehensive schema validation . The authorization server MUST abort processing and return invalid_authorization_details if the request contains an unknown authorization details type, an object with unknown fields, fields of the wrong type, or fields with invalid values. This is one of the few RFCs that explicitly mandates four distinct categories of schema validation failure.

**RFC 9207** Authorization Server Issuer Identification (2022) requires clients to extract the iss parameter from authorization responses and compare it using simple string comparison per RFC 3986 §6.2.1. If the value does not match, clients MUST reject the response and MUST NOT proceed. Clients MUST NOT allow multiple authorization servers to use the same issuer identifier.

**RFC 9101** JWT-Secured Authorization Request (2021) mandates signature validation against a key associated with the client in §6.2, requires algorithm verification per RFC 8725 §§3.1–3.2, and enforces that client_id values in the request parameter and Request Object claim MUST be identical — a cross-parameter consistency check.

**RFC 9126** Pushed Authorization Requests (2021) requires authorization servers to validate pushed requests exactly as they would authorization requests sent to the authorization endpoint, including redirect URI matching. IETF New redirect URIs MUST only be accepted from authenticated clients.

My take on this is a bit broader, Josh.

**_Normalization and validation, escaping and encoding, and sanitization are all important defensive techniques, but none of them are universal. The correct control depends on the nature of the data, the interpreter or sink involved, and the specific failure mode being prevented._**

So if we move in this direction, I would want to make sure the demotion of validation to “business logic only” is fully unwound. The current V1.3 introduction text is:

> The ideal protection against using untrusted content in an unsafe context is to use context-specific encoding or escaping, which maintains the same semantic meaning of the unsafe content but renders it safe for use in that particular context, as discussed in more detail in the previous section.

I propose updating it to:

I think we are still talking past each other slightly, so let me clarify the architectural point.

**_Validation, encoding/escaping, and sanitization are three different defensive techniques that address different classes of security failure, and none of them are subordinate to the others_**.

Validation is not merely business logic. In many security-critical systems it is the primary security control, including examples already discussed such as OAuth redirect URI validation (RFC 9700), WebAuthn origin validation, JWT claim validation, and URL protocol allowlists.

**_In these scenarios encoding or sanitization cannot solve the problem because the issue is semantic correctness of the data, not interpreter confusion._** Encoding is the primary defense for interpreter-based injection such as classic HTML XSS. Sanitization is typically a fallback where rejection is impractical, such as rich HTML input.

The concern I have with the proposed text is that it unintentionally frames validation as a secondary control that only applies “in some cases.” From a security architecture perspective that is inaccurate and risks reinforcing the critical misconception that validation is only business logic.

**_A more accurate framing would be that validation, encoding/escaping, and sanitization are all first-class defensive techniques, and the correct control depends on the data flow, interpreter, and threat model. Validation enforces security invariants on data, encoding protects interpreters, and sanitization removes unsafe constructs when rejection is not possible. All three are primary controls depending on the threat model._**

When it comes to continuous validation at every tier, that is a secondary point here. That guidance comes mostly from the zero trust world, especially NIST SP 800-228, section 2.6.1:

**_A service must validate that each request..._**

If you look at page 3, the document’s definition of “service” is broad enough to include internal and external services. And in section 1.1, it makes the zero trust position even clearer:

**_One of the most important implications of zero trust is that there is no meaningful distinction between an internal and external caller because the perimeter is the service instance itself._**

That kind of architecture is commonly understood to require validation at every service boundary.

That said, I do not think we need to push this point much further here. ASVS already covers this area reasonably well by requiring validation at service tiers. That is good enough for me.

**_My main concern is simpler: we need to fully fix the idea that validation is somehow not a security control. It is. We should stop framing validation as non-security logic or as a secondary defensive technique._**

I have been following this discussion. I see mostly agreement here, perhaps more than the thread suggests. I'd like to offer an observation that might help bridge the remaining gap.

Where everyone agrees (this list is larger than it appears):

- Sanitization should be allowlist based, blocklist only as last resort
- Encoding/escaping is the primary defense for interpreter injection
- Validation can be a primary security control (OAuth, JWT, WebAuthn examples demonstrate this)
- Sanitization is a last resort
- ASVS already covers validation as a security control in other sections

The actual disconnect. 

@tghosth is scoping V1.3 discussion to a specific data flow. Content that was already accepted into the system and is now being used in a dangerous context. Within that scope, he asked for examples of rejecting business valid data at point of use.

@jmanico is presenting an architectural perspective that validation is a first class security control and should not be framed as secondary. 

It seems both positions are addressing different scopes using different taxonomies, and that distinction has not been named explicitly.

I believe that the bridging principle here is context change. The reason previously accepted data becomes dangerous is that the context changes. A few categories of context change illustrate this:

- Interpreter/sink context change (V1.3's scope): data accepted as plain text is later rendered in HTML, used in an LDAP query, embedded in an OS command, etc. The data is unchanged; the interpreter changed.

- Temporal context change: certificates expire or get revoked, tokens expire, sessions time out. The data is structurally valid; the clock moved.

- Trust context change: revocation for affiliation change, federation trust removal, vendor risk status change. The data is unchanged; the relationship changed.

- Scope/privilege context change: a token with read scope presented to a write endpoint, a JWT audience mismatch. The data is unchanged; the required privilege changed.

For temporal, trust, and scope context changes, rejection is the appropriate control. A revoked certificate is still structurally valid and was legitimate from a business perspective when issued, but it gets rejected at point of use because the context changed. This happens at massive scale every day. That validates @jmanico's position that validation/rejection is a first class security control for already accepted data.

For interpreter/sink context changes (V1.3), encoding is usually the right answer, and where encoding is not possible, sanitization is the fallback. Rejection is possibly practical here too (Angular rejects javascript: URLs at render time, for example), but often is not (you cannot reject O'Brien from a SQL context). That validates @tghosth's position that V1.3 needs sanitization as a control.

Proposed V1.3 wording:

Data that has been accepted into an application may later be used in a context different from the one in which it was originally received. When the context changes (for example, from storage to use within an HTML page, an LDAP query, an OS command, or another interpreter), content which was safe in the original context may become dangerous in the new one.
The ideal protection is context specific encoding or escaping, which maintains the semantic meaning of the content while rendering it safe for the new context, as discussed above.

Where the new context allows it, validating the content against the safety requirements of that context and rejecting it if unsafe may also be appropriate. This is particularly practical when the data is received exclusively for use in a known security sensitive context (such as HTML from a WYSIWYG editor) or when the content can be evaluated against a well defined allowlist for the target context.

Where encoding or escaping is not possible and rejection is not practical, sanitization may be necessary. This involves keeping only characters or content known to be safe for the target context (allowlist based sanitization), or as a last resort, removing characters or content known to be dangerous (blocklist based sanitization). Sanitization may change the semantic meaning of the data, but for security reasons there may be no alternative.

Rejection is possibly practical here too (Angular rejects javascript: URLs at render time, for example), but often is not (you cannot reject O'Brien from a SQL context). That validates [@tghosth](https://github.com/tghosth)'s position that V1.3 needs sanitization as a control.
> 
> Proposed V1.3 wording:
> 
> Data that has been accepted into an application may later be used in a context different from the one in which it was originally received. When the context changes (for example, from storage to use within an HTML page, an LDAP query, an OS command, or another interpreter), content which was safe in the original context may become dangerous in the new one. The ideal protection is context specific encoding or escaping, which maintains the semantic meaning of the content while rendering it safe for the new context, as discussed above.
> 
> Where the new context allows it, validating the content against the safety requirements of that context and rejecting it if unsafe may also be appropriate. This is particularly practical when the data is received exclusively for use in a known security sensitive context (such as HTML from a WYSIWYG editor) or when the content can be evaluated against a well defined allowlist for the target context.
> 
> Where encoding or escaping is not possible and rejection is not practical, sanitization may be necessary. This involves keeping only characters or content known to be safe for the target context (allowlist based sanitization), or as a last resort, removing characters or content known to be dangerous (blocklist based sanitization). Sanitization may change the semantic meaning of the data, but for security reasons there may be no alternative.
> 
> Happy to iterate on this.

This post is poetry in motion. You did a fantastic job and I agree with most everything you said above. What a great way to sum up the situation. Well done!

> [@jmanico](https://github.com/jmanico), when people talk about XSS, they are generally thinking about classic HTML injection vectors, not JavaScript URL protocol abuse (regardless of popularity/statistics). Saying "one of the primary controls to stop real world XSS is input validation" is misleading because it conflates these two different things. Output encoding remains the primary defense for the XSS vectors that most developers think about.

Javascript URL's are one of the main classical attack vectors that causes XSS. A significant portion of modern XSS arises from JavaScript URL protocol abuse (javascript: URLs in href, src, etc.). Those are not solved by output encoding. Encoding does not change the browser’s interpretation of a URL scheme. In those cases the effective control is input validation that restricts allowed URL schemes.

**This is why treating encoding as the primary control is misleading**. Real systems require multiple defensive techniques depending on the interpreter involved:

- Output encoding → protects HTML/JS/CSS contexts from injection.
**_- Sanitization → required when untrusted HTML is intentionally allowed (e.g., WYSIWYG content)._**
- Input validation / allow-listing → required for structured data such as URLs, file types, identifiers, etc.

My reference for these statements is one of the CSP standard leads Michele Spagnuolo - Staff Information Security Engineer at google. You can reach him via https://miki.it/ or I can introduce you directly if you need a deeper reference.

There is a reason, why we removed the term XSS from ASVS - because the term is deprecated since 1996.

If one is talking about HTML injection and other JavaScript execution from src attribute, you can not find an agreement on defense methods that suits both.

So I recommend every security professional to use name, what says precisely what is the problem and what is the expected defense (such as HTML injection, HTML encoding) and if needed to someone, you may mention, it may be known as "XSS".

This is also example to Jim, why I'm not afraid to go to "industry definitions", because there is no clear definition for XSS.

@jmanico > Rejection is possibly practical here too (Angular rejects javascript: URLs at render time, for example), > The right defense (as we see in Angular) is to validate the legality and protocol of URL's. > So 1/3 of of all real world XSS is solved via input validation of URL's. > Or another way of saying it is: > One of the primary controls to stop real world XSS is input validation. > Input validation / allow-listing → required for structured data such as URLs, file types, identifiers, etc. For URLs, you’re saying that input validation is the best approach and you’re referencing Angular/DOMPurify. However, I’d like to point out that the actual implementation in the Angular GitHub codebase is different from what you’re describing. Based on the code, Angular performs runtime, context-aware sanitization, not classical input validation. In other words, Angular’s behavior is DOM sink protection, rather than rejecting the entire content/URL. According to the [Angular DomSanitizer documentation](https://angular.dev/api/platform-browser/DomSanitizer#description), values bound to URL contexts are sanitized during DOM binding. For example: Here is the [Angular Code for Sanitizing the URL](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/main/packages/core/src/sanitization/url_sanitizer.ts). Similarly, DOMPurify operate by sanitizing DOM elements and attributes, removing dangerous constructs (e.g., href="javascript:...") while preserving the rest of the content, rather than rejecting the entire input. Please review [DomPurify for URL Handling code](https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify/blob/8bcbf73ae7eb56e7b4f1300b66cf543342c7ee27/src/purify.ts#L1325) and refer the article for [DomPurify internals](https://dompurify.com/how-does-dompurify-ensure-that-sanitized-html-is-safe-for-injection-into-the-dom/). Validation is correct, but it belongs in the validation control category rather than the sanitization section. Please share your inputs .

Even if the primary attack vector could come from JavaScript execution from the src attribute, it is hard to believe that it makes it also the primary defense method in general against "XSS".

If you just compare how many times and for how many fields on the display layer an encoding is used and how many times a user-controlled src value in an exploitable src attribute exists in functionality, one can not say that the src attribute is so widespread that it outweighs all usage of encodings.

So phrases like "This is why treating encoding as the primary control is misleading," or "One of the primary controls to stop real-world XSS is input validation," as standalone lines are clearly misleading and must be avoided.

> Angular Code for Sanitizing the URL

The code for URL handling is a validator. If the URL pattern is malicious then Angular will reject the URL from rendering. Other aspects of Angular encode ({template rendering}) and other aspects of angular sanitize (the innerHTML sanitizer similar to DOMPurify).

> DOMPurify

This is also a combination of encoding, validation and HTML sanitization. But it's mostly a sanitizer.

Together there libraries are excellent patterns to stop XSS! :)
And when Angular sees the "unsafe:" protocol it's blocked. Good analysis. This is a validator. Angular sure is fantastic at stopping [XSS](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/cross_site_scripting)!

Thanks @jmanico  and @J-XL . 

> The function behavior is accept or reject. 
> The code for URL handling is a validator. If the URL pattern is malicious then Angular will reject the URL from rendering.

The `_sanitizeUrl` function calling it "validation" adds no practical value. the function job is purely to make the URL safe for DOM rendering that is a sanitization concern, not a validation concern. Prepending "unsafe:" is a transformation, not a rejection.

A validator rejects or accepts input unchanged. Angular `_sanitizeUrl` does neither. Allow-list based input validation means checking whether input conforms to an expected formula and rejecting it outright if it does not. The input is never modified. So I am sure that `_sanitizeUrl` is not a validator.

For the V1.3 section text, I would suggest to use word called "**context-aware sanitization**", as context-aware sanitization is a more accurate and useful framing than allowlist/blocklist. Validation is important but it is a separate concern, when discussing sanitization, the primary question is whether the sanitization is appropriate for the specific context it is being applied in. That principle naturally guides developers to the right mechanism without prescribing allowlist or blocklist universally. For Angular URL contexts, the framework behavior is better described as context-aware sanitization, not plain business-style validation.

I would propose below wording for V1.3 introduction text

Sanitization modifies or removes parts of data to make it safe for use in a specific context. Unlike encoding, which preserves the meaning of the data while making it safe to interpret, and validation, which accepts or rejects data without changing it, sanitization changes the data itself.

Effective sanitization must be context-aware. the right technique depends on the target interpreter or rendering context and the type of dangerous content. The goal is to ensure that only content that is safe for that context reaches the interpreter.

Sanitization is appropriate only when it is the correct control for the target context, such as when rendering user-supplied rich text HTML. Applying sanitization blindly in contexts where encoding, escaping, or parameterization is more appropriate is ineffective and may create a false sense of security. 


Please suggest, if it aligns with the expectations. Happy to discuss further or refine based on feedback.

For me, this exchange highlights something. I am not convinced we have clarified behavioral definitions in the standard's text. Let's take a minute to consider this.

@ajayojha noted that _sanitizeUrl performs a "transformation" (prepending "unsafe:") and therefore constitutes sanitization. That's worth examining more closely by looking at what the function actually produces.

The ASVS V1.3 text describes sanitization as "removing potentially dangerous characters or content" where the output "may change the semantic meaning of the input." The key word is "removing." Sanitization uses selective modification. Strips the dangerous parts. Keeps the safe parts. Returns usable (if altered) content. The HTML sanitizer that strips <script> tags but preserves < b > and < p > is the classic example. The output is a reduced but functional form of the input.

Angular's _sanitizeUrl does not do this. It has exactly 2 outcomes:

URL matches the safe pattern --> passes through unchanged
URL does not match --> entire URL is neutralized by prepending "unsafe:"

No selective removal. No partial preservation. The output of a failed check is not usable content. It is an unexecutable URL. That is functionally equivalent to rejection. The "unsafe:" prefix is a tombstone, not a modification.

Perhaps this discussion represents a good opportunity to consider adding explicit behavioral definitions to the ASVS glossary, giving all chapters a shared reference point (something like):

- 	Encoding/escaping transforms content so that the target interpreter treats it as data rather than instructions. The semantic meaning is preserved and the original content is fully represented in the output.

- 	Validation evaluates content against the safety or business requirements of a context and either accepts it unchanged or rejects it. No content is selectively modified. Rejection may take various forms (blocking, returning an error, neutralizing the input) but the defining characteristic is that accepted content passes through unmodified.

- 	Sanitization selectively modifies content, removing or altering the dangerous portions while preserving the safe portions. The output is a reduced but still functional version of the input. The semantic meaning may change.

Under these definitions, Angular's _sanitizeUrl is a validator despite its function name. In this case, the function name is a documentation artifact, not a behavioral description. The code performs accept/reject. It does not selectively modify.

Having crisp behavioral definitions makes this decision tree more actionable for developers. At minimum, agreeing on these definitions gives us a shared foundation for this discussion. This thread itself demonstrates the need. We have seemingly arrived at different classifications for the same function. This leads me to think we are working from different implicit definitions.
